newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Rival Liberia factions make peace, agree to disarm.
newsitem.headline: Rival Liberia factions make peace, agree to disarm.

text.p: The two factions of Liberia's ULIMO militia at the centre of fighting in Monrovia this year agreed on Friday to reunite and disarm their guerrillas.
Leaders of the ULIMO-K and ULIMO-J factions signed an accord in Monrovia's Executive Mansion, the presidential office complex coveted by fighters in seven years of civil war.
In the agreement the two factions undertook to "cease all armed and political hostilities and remove all road blocks and checkpoints within our respective areas". They also agreed
"immediate disengagement of our forces to be assembled at designated locations for disarmament and demobilisation".
The move marked a signifcicant step in renewed efforts to rescue a 1995 accord to end the Liberian conflict.
Fighting in April and May derailed a regional plan for disarmament and elections. Warlords signed an accord in Nigeria on August 19 under pressure from West African heads of state.

"We want to assure our citizens that the two leaders of the two ULIMO are sincerely making peace today," declared ULIMO-J leader General Roosevelt Johnson at the ceremony. "We are not bluffing and this message will go down to our fighters that enough is enough and that this is the time for peace."
"We fought in April among ourselves because we have not learnt our lesson or realized our purpose," ULIMO-K leader Alhaji Kromah said.
ULIMO-J invaded from Sierra Leone in 1991 before it split in 1993 over power-sharing.
The two guerrilla leaders shook hands and posed for cameras joined by their followers chanting old guerrilla songs.
The ceremony took place on the eve of what is billed as the biggest disarment drive by the West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG since April's fighting.

ECOMOG field commander, Nigerian general Samuel Victor Malu, told reporters Kromah's guerrillas would start handing in their weapons at a ceremony on Saturday in their stronghold town of Voinjama on the border with Guinea.

The number of guerrillas or the type and quantity of weapons involved was not immediately clear but Kromah termed the move as a fulfilment of his decision to disarm all his guerrillas by September 30.
There are an estimated 60,000 armed guerrillas in Liberia, with chief warlord Charles Taylor who started the civil war in 1989 commanding the largest force.
Taylor has promised to start disarming his men in two weeks' time when he expects to demobilise about 3,000.
Officials from the United States embassy are due to observe Saturday's disarmament ceremony along with representatives of international relief organisations.
Liberia was founded by freed American slaves in 1847 as Africa's first republic and the United States remains the most influential foreign power in the couny.
